24d5c4737a2e69cd	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)?	Coronary Artery Disease, also known as ischemic heart disease, is a condition where plaque builds up in the coronary arteries, restricting blood flow to the heart. It is the leading cause of death globally, accounting for 16% of total deaths.	CAD definition epidemiology subject:cardiology
24f0666135d1785c	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are the global mortality statistics for cardiovascular disease?	According to WHO 2019 statistics, cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of mortality accounting for 18.5 million deaths annually, far exceeding cancer (10 million) and respiratory diseases (under 4 million).	epidemiology mortality global-health subject:cardiology
6dd3e8f3d2499c0c	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the double burden of disease in South Africa and low/middle-income countries?	The double burden refers to the simultaneous high prevalence of both infectious diseases (tuberculosis, AIDS) and non-communicable diseases (lifestyle-related conditions like CAD, hypertension, diabetes).	epidemiology public-health disease-burden subject:cardiology
df45cad8b30a1d61	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the most lethal manifestation of Coronary Artery Disease?	Myocardial infarction (heart attack) is the most lethal and dangerous manifestation of CAD. It is a medical emergency caused by complete or near-complete blockage of a coronary artery.	CAD complications myocardial-infarction subject:cardiology
afb3d400e878cbdd	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the key message about CAD prevention and modification?	CAD is a disease of lifestyle that can be modified through choices about diet and physical activity. It can also be managed with pharmacological therapies and mechanical interventions (angioplasty, stenting, bypass surgery). Leading a judicious lifestyle can delay or prevent CAD onset.	CAD prevention management subject:cardiology
21a30b799e85d200	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are the main clinical manifestations of CAD?	The main manifestations are: (1) Stable/Chronic coronary syndrome (stable angina), (2) Acute coronary syndrome including ST-elevation MI and non-ST elevation MI, (3) Unstable angina, (4) Silent ischemia, and (5) Sudden cardiac death.	CAD clinical-manifestations presentation subject:cardiology
9f7169b16f6612c1	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	Why is CAD now called Chronic Coronary Syndrome?	CAD is called chronic coronary syndrome because the disease starts early (in teen years or even earlier) but remains clinically silent for many years. Evidence of disease appears as fatty streaks in arteries from childhood, becoming manifest typically after age 35, most commonly between ages 50-80.	CAD pathophysiology disease-progression subject:cardiology
f077bfe46b10983b	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the difference between ST-elevation MI (STEMI) and non-ST elevation MI?	In STEMI, the thrombus causes total occlusion of the coronary vessel, making it a medical emergency with rapid myocardial death. In non-STEMI, the thrombus is not completely occlusive, allowing some blood flow; it is less time-dependent but still requires urgent treatment.	acute-coronary-syndrome myocardial-infarction STEMI subject:cardiology
891dac470a8f61d4	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are non-modifiable risk factors for CAD?	Non-modifiable risk factors are: (1) Age - prevalence increases after age 35; (2) Male gender - higher lifetime risk; (3) Family history of early CAD (father/brother <55 years or mother/sister <65 years); (4) Certain ethnicities including Indian, Afrikaans, Ashkenazi Jewish, and Scottish populations.	risk-factors non-modifiable epidemiology subject:cardiology
e3b20df1a09b27a1	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are the lifetime risks for CAD development by gender after age 40?	Men have a 49% lifetime risk of developing CAD after age 40 years, while women have a 32% lifetime risk. After menopause, the prevalence becomes equivalent between genders.	risk-factors gender epidemiology subject:cardiology
3198b300b9501713	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the relationship between family history and CAD risk?	Family history of CAD below age 50 years indicates increased risk. Specifically: if father or brother diagnosed before 55 years, or mother or sister diagnosed before 65 years of age, these individuals are at additional risk.	risk-factors family-history genetics subject:cardiology
df10e1d8fda1607a	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the most prevalent modifiable risk factor for CAD?	Hypertension is the most prevalent modifiable risk factor, with approximately one out of every three individuals globally having hypertension.	risk-factors modifiable hypertension subject:cardiology
eec8f074bcb7d602	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	How does diabetes affect CAD risk and outcomes?	Diabetes mellitus (both Type 1 and Type 2) increases the rate of CAD by more than 2.5 times compared to non-diabetics. Although hypertension and hyperlipidemia are more common, diabetes is a more severe condition, leading to greater disease burden and poorer outcomes in CAD patients.	risk-factors diabetes CAD-outcomes subject:cardiology
8646ded1b911752f	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the CAD risk increase from secondhand smoke exposure?	Non-smokers exposed to secondhand smoking have a 25-30% increased risk of CAD compared to those never exposed to cigarette smoke. This is why smoking is banned in public areas - not to protect smokers, but to protect non-smokers.	risk-factors smoking secondhand-smoke subject:cardiology
6b1e6a9d0cc514ae	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What dietary factors increase CAD risk?	Dietary risk factors include: (1) Added sugars in soft drinks and sweetened beverages - associated with >20% higher MI risk; (2) Saturated and trans fats; (3) Excess red meat and processed meats (sausages, cured meats); (4) Overall poor diet quality.	risk-factors diet nutrition subject:cardiology
9e31ffd6af394aac	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the relationship between obesity and CAD?	Obesity is an independent risk factor for CAD and also increases the risk of developing other risk factors like hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and Type 2 diabetes. This effect is particularly pronounced with abdominal obesity.	risk-factors obesity metabolic subject:cardiology
013ee4525d42addc	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are less recognized risk factors for CAD?	Less recognized risk factors include: (1) Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) - now the commonest cause of cirrhosis; (2) Chronic kidney disease - increases CAD incidence and mortality; (3) Inflammatory conditions (lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease); (4) HIV infection.	risk-factors comorbidities inflammatory subject:cardiology
fb6fc0f5e4e93028	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the Framingham Risk Score and what are its components?	The Framingham Risk Score is one of the oldest risk assessment tools. It considers: age, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, systolic blood pressure (treated or untreated), and smoking status. It provides a 10-year likelihood of developing cardiovascular disease including CAD, stroke, and peripheral artery disease.	risk-assessment Framingham tools subject:cardiology
6a5f5991e678e96e	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	Why is the Framingham Risk Score not useful in certain populations?	The Framingham Risk Score is not useful in diabetics or those with familial hyperlipidemia because these individuals are already at higher risk simply by virtue of having these conditions. Risk scoring is unnecessary when baseline risk is already elevated.	risk-assessment limitations diabetes subject:cardiology
15d62fc01f190b9f	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are the Framingham Risk Score categories and their implications?	Risk score categories: (1) Score <3 = Low risk; (2) Score 3-15 = Moderate risk; (3) Score >15, especially >30 = High risk requiring pharmacotherapy in addition to lifestyle measures. Scores >30 require aggressive risk factor control to minimize MI and death risk.	risk-assessment stratification management subject:cardiology
c53b8f56342b6939	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	Who are considered very high-risk for cardiovascular events without needing risk scoring?	Individuals at very high risk who do NOT require risk scoring include: (1) Those with established atherosclerotic disease in any vascular territory; (2) Type 2 diabetes with other risk factors; (3) Type 1 diabetes with proteinuria; (4) Familial/genetic hyperlipidemia; (5) Severe chronic kidney disease (stages 4-5); (6) Asymptomatic individuals with evidence of atherosclerotic plaques on imaging.	risk-assessment high-risk very-high-risk subject:cardiology
256d61c513b5ff94	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the significance of atherosclerotic disease in multiple vascular territories?	If atherosclerotic disease is established in one vascular territory (coronary, cerebrovascular, peripheral arterial), the likelihood of having it in other vascular beds is high. This is why individuals with established atherosclerosis in any location automatically have very high overall cardiovascular risk.	atherosclerosis disease-progression risk-stratification subject:cardiology
2f2d486831358803	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What defines familial/genetic hyperlipidemia risk?	Severe familial hyperlipidemia automatically places individuals at high CAD risk. It is defined by: total cholesterol >7.5 mmol/L or LDL cholesterol >5 mmol/L (LDL is 'bad cholesterol'). This population is particularly common among people of Dutch descent in South Africa, with approximately 300,000 severely affected individuals.	hyperlipidemia genetics familial subject:cardiology
ede7fa5e22fe5eb7	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the pathophysiology of chronic coronary syndrome?	In chronic coronary syndrome, a plaque composed of lipid, inflammatory cells, and smooth muscle cells causes >50-70% lumen stenosis in a coronary artery. This narrowing limits blood flow downstream, manifesting as ischemic chest pain (angina) only when the vessel is narrowed >70%.	pathophysiology chronic-syndrome stenosis subject:cardiology
b8628a713ce65a8a	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the pathophysiology of acute coronary syndrome in STEMI?	In STEMI, a plaque ruptures and a large thrombus forms on the rupture site, causing complete occlusion of the coronary vessel. This is a true emergency because there is no blood flow downstream and myocytes rapidly begin to die (myocardial infarction).	pathophysiology acute-syndrome STEMI thrombus subject:cardiology
baf20a09394cfbc2	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the pathophysiology of acute coronary syndrome in non-STEMI?	In non-STEMI, a long-standing plaque fissures or ruptures and a thrombus forms, but the thrombus is not completely occlusive. Stenosis increases from 50-70% to ~90%, but some blood flow remains. Infarction occurs when bits of the clot break off and block smaller downstream vessels.	pathophysiology acute-syndrome non-STEMI subject:cardiology
7b6b569c12ae220e	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is stable angina and how is it defined?	Stable angina is now called Chronic Coronary Syndrome. It is defined as angina where the symptom characteristics have remained unchanged for the preceding 60 days. This distinction is important to differentiate it from unstable angina, where symptoms are changing or new.	stable-angina chronic-syndrome definition subject:cardiology
cf97b28686f0f99f	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	How is angina diagnosed?	Angina is diagnosed by history and history alone. The diagnosis is made based on the patient's description of symptoms, not on any investigation or test. ECG, stress testing, or imaging can support the diagnosis but are not required for diagnosis.	diagnosis angina clinical subject:cardiology
15a4a656ff373d2d	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What are the three criteria for typical angina?	Typical angina must satisfy all three criteria: (1) Chest discomfort described as constriction in the front of chest, radiating to neck, jaw, shoulder, or arm(s); (2) Provoked by physical exertion or emotional stress; (3) Rapidly relieved by rest or nitrates within 5 minutes.	angina typical criteria subject:cardiology

5e4d1eb62eace0b4	Basic	Corpus::Cardiology::Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)	What is the Canadian Cardiovascular Society Classification of Angina?	The CCS Classification grades angina severity: (1) Class I - Angina only with very strenuous exertion; (2) Class II - Angina with moderate exertion; (3) Class III - Angina with mild exertion; (4) Class IV - Angina at rest. Treatment is lifelong because CAD is a chronic disease process that continues throughout life. The underlying atherosclerotic disease persists and requires ongoing management.	management treatment chronic-disease subject:cardiology

63c1f6fbe12b2365	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What are the major pathophysiologic mechanisms for ascites formation?	Four main mechanisms: (1) Increased hydrostatic pressure from portal hypertension (cirrhosis, hepatic vein thrombosis, IVC obstruction, constrictive pericarditis, congestive heart failure); (2) Decreased colloidal osmotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, protein-losing enteropathy); (3) Increased permeability from peritoneal disease (tuberculosis peritonitis, bacterial peritonitis, malignancy metastases); (4) Leakage of fluid from organs (biliary leak, pancreatic ascites, chylous ascites, urinary ascites).	ascites pathophysiology mechanisms subject:gastroenterology

49822418e185e638	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What is the serum ascitic albumin gradient (SAG) and how is it calculated?	The SAG is calculated by subtracting ascitic albumin from serum albumin. SAG is the most useful test to distinguish causes of ascites. A high SAG (≥1.1 g/dL or ≥11 g/L) indicates portal hypertension in most cases. A low SAG (<1.1 g/dL or <11 g/L) suggests other causes like tuberculosis, serositis, nephrotic syndrome, or peritoneal metastases. The SAG should always be ordered when ascitic fluid is obtained.	ascites serum-gradient diagnostic-test subject:gastroenterology
50730c9dd7ce46ae	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and how is it diagnosed? ae5038246ffd0a17	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What does lymphocyte-predominant ascitic fluid indicate? 18a9593e811f2a30	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What is the pathophysiology of ascites in cirrhosis and portal hypertension?	In cirrhosis, hepatic architecture is distorted with increased hepatic vascular tone, causing portal hypertension. This activates vasodilation mechanisms mediated by nitric oxide overproduction, which dilates splanchnic and peripheral vessels. This causes underfilling of the systemic arterial space and triggers baroreceptor activation, increasing renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release. Sodium and water retention develops, leading to ascites. Simultaneously, splanchnic vasodilation increases lymph production, which exceeds transport capacity and leaks into the peritoneal cavity.	ascites pathophysiology cirrhosis subject:gastroenterology
e059be13ece39d2e	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What is the first step in managing ascites?	The first step is to diagnose the underlying cause of ascites, as treatment should target the etiology. For TB peritonitis, TB treatment is needed. For malignancy, chemotherapy may help. For heart failure, diuretics are required. For portal hypertension from cirrhosis, treatment aims to minimize ascites formation since cirrhosis cannot be reversed.	ascites management etiology subject:gastroenterology
57e4605de920214d	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What dietary modifications are used in ascites management?	Sodium restriction is the cornerstone of dietary management for ascites due to portal hypertension. Patients should be restricted to approximately 2 grams of sodium per day. 9a19c32b47b45f8d	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What is spironolactone and why is it used in ascites?	Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist used as first-line diuretic therapy for ascites. It blocks the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the renal collecting duct, thus promoting sodium and water excretion. Starting dose is 100 mg daily, titrated up to a maximum of 400 mg daily. Side effects include fluctuations in potassium, sodium, and creatinine (requiring electrolyte/renal function monitoring), muscle cramps, and gynecomatia (even with early/long-term use).	ascites management spironolactone subject:gastroenterology

Furosemide is a loop diuretic used as second-line or adjunct therapy for ascites. Starting dose is approximately 40 mg daily, titrated up to a maximum of 160 mg daily. 4b3147738fd7626b	Basic	Corpus::Gastroenterology::An Approach To Ascites	What are the principles of diuretic dose adjustment in ascites? The strategy by which individuals in contact with a case of confirmed or suspected pulmonary TB are screened for the presence of TB infection or disease, with the aim of offering either anti-tuberculosis preventive therapy or anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy.	contact-tracing screening subject:paediatrics
5e9a1c3f7b2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	Define reverse contact-tracing.	The strategy adopted when a child is the index case with active TB, and the potential source case (usually an adult or older child in the index case's home environment) is sought by symptom screening and/or chest radiography of household contacts.	contact-tracing reverse-tracing subject:paediatrics
3a8f1b5e9c2d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What are the key factors determining TB disease progression in children?	Age of the child (<5 years of age), time since exposure/infection (±1 year), and immune status of the child.	pathogenesis risk-factors subject:paediatrics
7c4a2f1e9b5d3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the typical size range of MTB bacilli?	MTB bacilli range in length from 1-10 μm (micrometers).	microbiology mtb-characteristics subject:paediatrics
2e5b8a1f7c3d4a9c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	Why are children <10 years of age less likely to transmit TB?	Children <10 years of age rarely develop lung cavities, and therefore are less likely to transmit the TB organism.	transmission pathogenesis subject:paediatrics
9a1c5f3b7e2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What major pathogenic components does MTB have in its cell wall?	Heat shock proteins (highly immunogenic), cord factor (glycolipid that induces granuloma), and LAM (lipoarabinomannan).	pathogenesis cell-wall immunology subject:paediatrics
4d7e2a1f9b5c3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What percentage of bacterial mass does LAM represent?	LAM (lipoarabinomannan) represents 15% of the bacterial mass.	pathogenesis lam immunology subject:paediatrics
1f9a4c3b7e2d5a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What are the effects of LAM on immune response?	LAM inhibits macrophage activation by interferon gamma, and induces macrophage to secrete IL-10 (suppresses TB-induced T cell proliferation) and TNF alpha (causing fever, weight loss and tissue damage).	pathogenesis lam immunology subject:paediatrics
5c2f8b1a9e3d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the Ghon focus and when does it develop?	The Ghon focus is the initial inflammatory reaction site in the lung parenchyma where TB organism deposits. It develops within 2-3 weeks of infection and may resolve and calcify.	pathophysiology ghon-complex subject:paediatrics
8e1a5d3c7f2b4a9c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the Ghon complex?	The Ghon complex includes the Ghon focus in the lung parenchyma together with enlarged regional hilar lymph nodes. It represents a controlled and retained non-proliferating Mycobacterium.	pathophysiology ghon-complex latent-tb subject:paediatrics
3a9f1c5e8b2d7a4c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What are the three possible outcomes of TB infection in the primary phase?	1) Can be cleared by host immunity (primary infection). 2) Suppressed into inactive form (latent TB) with calcified scar visible on X-ray. 3) Spread (active TB).	pathophysiology primary-infection subject:paediatrics
7d2c4f1b9a5e3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is fibrocaseous TB?	TB in which hydrolytic enzymes dissolve MTB in larger lesions surrounded by fibrous capsule. Fibrocaseous nodules contain viable mycobacterium and pose lifelong risk for reactivation.	pathophysiology active-tb subject:paediatrics
9f3a1e5b7c2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is proliferative TB granuloma?	Granuloma with effective killing of Mycobacterium due to proliferating lymphocytes, plasma cells, outer rim of fibrosis, and low bacillary load.	pathophysiology granuloma subject:paediatrics
2e8c4a1f5b9d3a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is exudative TB granuloma?	Granuloma with higher bacillary load, caseating necrosis, and progression of infection if not treated. Also called caseating granuloma/fibrocaseous.	pathophysiology granuloma active-disease subject:paediatrics
4a7f2d1c9e5b3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	List the constitutional symptoms of TB infection.	Fever and night sweats, weight loss and failure to thrive, fatigue and anorexia.	symptoms clinical-presentation subject:paediatrics
1c9b5a3e8f2d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What number of symptom criteria is highly suggestive of TB diagnosis?	2 or more of the TB symptom criteria are highly suggestive of TB diagnosis.	symptoms diagnosis subject:paediatrics
6a2f8c1e5b9d3a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the symptom criterion for persistent cough in TB screening?	Persistent or non-remitting cough/wheeze >2 weeks (unresponsive to appropriate antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia).	symptoms respiratory screening subject:paediatrics
3e7a1f5b8c2d4a9c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the symptom criterion for weight loss in TB screening?	Documented low weight or failure to thrive (FTT) for the past 3 months (especially if not responding to intervention).	symptoms growth screening subject:paediatrics
8f1c4a5b9e2d7a3c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What are the clinical hypersensitivity phenomena occurring 4-12 weeks after primary TB infection?	1) TST conversion. 2) Erythema nodosum (raised red, painful macules on anterior lower legs). 3) Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (raised red nodule on limbus with conjunctival injection). 4) Poncet's polyarthritis.	hypersensitivity clinical-signs subject:paediatrics

2a5f9c1e7b3d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the role of CD4 Th cells in TB infection? 7c4a1f9e5b2d3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the role of CD8+ T suppressor cells in TB granuloma formation?	CD8+ T suppressor cells kill macrophages that are infected, leading to caseating granuloma formation (delayed hypersensitivity reaction).	immunity cellular-immunity subject:paediatrics
3e8b2c1a9f5d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	Why can granulomas be paradoxical in TB control?	While granulomas are acidic, anaerobic, extracellular environments that inhibit MTB growth, they can also cause tissue damage if they fail to contain the disease, leading to spread and further tissue destruction.	pathophysiology granuloma subject:paediatrics
1a7f4d5c2e9b3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What X-ray finding indicates controlled primary TB infection?	Calcified scar in the lung parenchyma and/or hilar lymph nodes (Ghon focus/complex) indicating controlled and retained non-proliferating Mycobacterium.	imaging primary-infection subject:paediatrics
8d2a5e1c9f3b4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is the TST (Tuberculin Skin Test) reading timeframe?	The TST is read after 48-72 hours.	diagnosis tst interpretation subject:paediatrics
4c9b1f3e7a5d2a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What does a positive TST indicate?	A positive TST indicates TB infection (not necessarily TB disease). It measures hypersensitivity to tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD).	diagnosis tst interpretation subject:paediatrics
2f8a4c1b9e5d3a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What does a positive TST signify in children <5 years or HIV-infected children?	In children <5 years or HIV-infected children, a positive TST indicates recent infection and is a risk factor for progression to active TB disease.	diagnosis tst risk-factors subject:paediatrics
5a1e7c3f9b2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What conditions can cause a false negative TST?	HIV infection, malnutrition, severe viral infections (measles, chicken pox), cancer, immunosuppressive drugs (steroids), severe disseminated TB, and recent TB exposure (2-3 months conversion window period).	diagnosis tst false-negative subject:paediatrics
9c3b2a5f7e1d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	How should a positive TST be interpreted in endemic countries after BCG vaccine? 6d5a1e9f7c2b4a3c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is BCG vaccine derived from?	BCG vaccine is a live attenuated vaccine derived from Mycobacterium bovis.	immunization bcg vaccine-types subject:paediatrics

7a9f3c1b5e2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What protection does BCG provide in TB-endemic countries?	BCG provides children with a degree of protection against disseminated and severe forms of TB (TB meningitis and miliary TB).	immunization bcg protection subject:paediatrics
1e4c9a2f8b5d3a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	Should asymptomatic HIV-exposed babies receive BCG vaccine?	Yes. Due to high TB burden, it is recommended that routine BCG vaccination be given at birth to asymptomatic HIV-exposed babies, but they must be monitored closely for BCG-related adverse events.	immunization bcg hiv subject:paediatrics
4b7d2c1f9a5e3a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	List the danger signs requiring urgent hospital referral for TB.	Severe respiratory distress (TB pneumonia), severe wheezing not responding to bronchodilators (severe airway compression), signs/symptoms of meningism and seizures (TBM), hepatosplenomegaly (disseminated TB), breathlessness and peripheral edema (pericardial effusion), severe pulmonary disease and malnutrition, distended abdomen with/without ascites (TB abdomen), and angulation of the spine gibbous (TB spine).	emergency danger-signs complications subject:paediatrics
8a1f5c3e9b2d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	Why is TB diagnosis more complex in HIV-infected children?	TB disease diagnosis is indistinguishable from other HIV-related lung diseases, symptoms such as chronic cough, weight loss, and persistent fever are common to both, and TST is frequently negative.	hiv-coinfection diagnosis subject:paediatrics
2c8e3a1f9b5d4a7c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	List the differential diagnoses of pulmonary TB in HIV-infected children. Chest X-ray abnormalities consistent with active TB, clinical picture only (empiric treatment), histological and biochemical tests suggestive of TB, or a combination of the above due to paucibacillary nature of TB in children.	diagnosis clinical-diagnosis subject:paediatrics

3f7c1a9e5b2d4a8c	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::2024 TUBERCULOSIS	What is urine LAM testing?	Detection of LAM (lipoarabinomannan) levels in the urine. a1f2e3d4c5b6a7f8	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::ASTHMA 2021 CONSENSUS GUIDELINE	How is asthma diagnosed in children?	Asthma is diagnosed in children who present with episodes of variable expiratory airflow limitation. It remains a largely clinical diagnosis, which should be supported by lung function testing in school-aged children. Symptoms may include episodic wheeze, shortness of breath, difficult or laboured breathing, chest tightness and reduced activity with or without cough.	asthma diagnosis subject:paediatrics
b2g3f4e5d6c7a8b9	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::ASTHMA 2021 CONSENSUS GUIDELINE	What symptoms improve asthma diagnosis?	Symptoms that improve after correct use of a rapid-acting inhaled bronchodilator support asthma diagnosis. Chronic airway inflammation and variable expiratory airflow limitation define asthma.	asthma bronchodilator diagnosis subject:paediatrics
c3h4g5f6e7d8a9c0	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::ASTHMA 2021 CONSENSUS GUIDELINE	Wheezing frequency supporting asthma?	Events that occur more frequently (>3 episodes per year) and that last longer (>10 days at a time) may indicate an asthma diagnosis.	asthma wheezing frequency subject:paediatrics
d4i5h6g7f8e9a0b1	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::ASTHMA 2021 CONSENSUS GUIDELINE	Temporal pattern supporting asthma diagnosis?	Wheeze that does not only occur during airway infections, but also in response to other triggers in-between infections supports an asthma diagnosis. Events that persist after 3 years of age, night-time worsening, and association with exercise or environmental change (e.g. cold air exposure) further support an asthma diagnosis.	asthma triggers temporal-pattern subject:paediatrics
e5j6i7h8g9f0a1b2	Basic	Corpus::Paediatrics::ASTHMA 2021 CONSENSUS GUIDELINE	Four diagnostic steps for asthma <6 years?	Step 1: History taking (most important). Step 2: Exclude an alternative reason for wheezing episodes. Step 3: Assess inflammation (therapeutic trial with ICS). Step 4: Seek objective evidence of variable expiratory airflow limitation.	asthma diagnosis steps under-6-years subject:paediatrics

ne086hiv-bpcr-positive01	Basic		Describe the management pathway for a neonate with positive birth PCR.	1) Actively trace positive BPCR and link to care; 2) Post-test counselling for mother; 3) Baseline assessment (clinical and lab: HIV PCR, CD4, FBC/Hb, AST); 4) ART adherence counselling; 5) Start ART same day when baby tolerates enteral feeds (AZT/3TC/NVP).	hiv neonatal-treatment management-pathway subject:paediatrics-neonatal

ne115sexual-protect01	Basic		What sexual precautions should pregnant women take?	Use male latex condoms consistently and correctly. ne117malaria-prevent01	Basic		What is the prevention measure for malaria in pregnant women in endemic areas?	Always use insecticide-treated bed nets if living in a malaria endemic area.	prevention malaria subject:paediatrics-neonatal
ne118child-contact01	Basic		What precautions should pregnant women take with children with respiratory/rash symptoms? 40134ebc497ed2a7	Basic	Corpus::Rheumatology::Spondyloarthropathies	What is the treatment approach for enteropathic spondylarthropathy?	Treatment: (1) NSAIDs for axial pain and lower back pain (use with caution in IBD), (2) Sulfasalazine for peripheral arthritis, (3) Steroids for peripheral arthritis, (4) Anti-TNF drugs (particularly infliximab) benefit both arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease.	enteropathic-arthritis treatment NSAIDs anti-TNF subject:rheumatology
64c67d9293c2d198	Basic	Corpus::Rheumatology::Spondyloarthropathies	What are the spinal manifestations of enteropathic spondylarthropathy?	Spinal manifestations include syndesmophytes (bony bridges) that cross from one vertebral body to another, extending on either side of vertebrae, eventually progressing to involve more vertebral bodies and resulting in complete fusion and stiffening of the spine.	enteropathic-arthritis spinal-involvement imaging subject:rheumatology
bdf3a6a4d5294e41	Basic	Corpus::Rheumatology::Spondyloarthropathies	What is the difference between mechanical and inflammatory back pain?	Mechanical back pain is differentiated from inflammatory back pain in SpA by: (1) Age of onset (inflammatory less than 40-45 years), (2) Insidious vs acute onset, (3) Chronic duration (3+ months), (4) Morning stiffness pattern and improvement with activity, (5) Nocturnal pain, (6) No improvement with rest.	back-pain differentiation clinical-assessment subject:rheumatology
16961d054d30503f	Basic	Corpus::Rheumatology::Spondyloarthropathies	What are the vertebral erosive changes seen in SpA?	Early erosive changes at the corners of vertebral bodies are associated with SpA, with formation of syndesmophytes at the edge of vertebral bodies, progressing to bridge adjacent vertebrae and eventually resulting in bamboo spine with complete vertebral fusion.	SpA vertebral-pathology imaging subject:rheumatology
